what: The Macro Calculator estimates how many calories you need each day and how to split them into protein, carbohydrates and fat. It uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, which is widely used by dietitians to estimate resting energy needs.
You can use kilograms and centimeters or pounds, feet and inches, pick a goal from weight loss to muscle gain, and choose a preset eating style or your own percentages.
uses: Get a daily number for losing, keeping or gaining weight.
See grams of each macro per day and per meal.
Compare balanced, high-protein, lower-carb and keto splits.
Copy your targets into a food tracking app.
tutorial: Pick "Metric (kg, cm)" or "Imperial (lb, ft, in)". Numbers you typed are converted.
Choose your sex and type your age, weight and height.
Choose the activity level that matches a normal week and your goal.
Pick a preset or "Custom" and type percentages that add up to 100.
Type how many meals you eat to see grams per meal.
See daily calories, grams of protein, carbs and fat, and the table with calories and shares.
features: A modern, widely used formula for resting calories.
From little exercise (× 1.2) to very hard (× 1.9).
Balanced, higher carb, high protein, lower carb, keto or your own.
Grams per meal for the number of meals you choose.

example.title: Worked example
example.text: A 30-year-old woman, 70 kg and 170 cm: 10 × 70 + 6.25 × 170 − 5 × 30 − 161 = 1,451.5 kcal at rest. With moderate exercise (× 1.55) that is about 2,250 kcal a day. A balanced 30/40/30 split gives about 169 g protein, 225 g carbs and 75 g fat.

tips: Weigh yourself at the same time of day for a steady number.
Pick the activity level for a typical week, not your best week.
Check progress after 2–3 weeks and adjust calories by about 5–10% if needed.
problems: A red message about the split
Custom percentages must add up to 100.
Check the activity level; many people choose one level too high.
Pick a gentler goal such as "Lose slowly".
